questions.a: Babies are overrated because adults actually learn faster at first. A child knows only about 20 words after 18 months, while adults benefit from transfer and better general cognitive skills. Adults do worse only in ultimate attainment, since they rarely become native-like.

questions.q: What is transfer, and how does it make the Hindi dental and retroflex contrast hard for English speakers?
questions.a: Transfer is the use of L1 processes and representations for an L2. English speakers hear both Hindi dental and retroflex consonants through their single alveolar category. So the two sounds seem the same, and transfer makes the L2 contrast harder to learn.

questions.q: Why are Chinese classifiers hard for native English speakers?
questions.a: They are hard because Chinese requires different classifiers for different kinds of nouns, such as objects with handles or flat objects. English determiners do not depend on what kind of thing a noun names. So English speakers have learned to ignore the cues that classifiers depend on.

questions.q: What did de Groot and Keijzer (2000) do and find?
questions.a: Dutch speakers learned made-up words paired with Dutch words that varied in cognate status and concreteness. Cognates were learned more rapidly and remembered more easily after a week without training. So cognate status helps the very earliest stages of second language word learning.

questions.q: Why did de Groot and Keijzer’s productive test make the study more convincing?
questions.a: A receptive test alone would not be impressive, because many cognate meanings, such as gitaar, could be guessed without training. The productive test asked for the made-up word itself, given the Dutch word. So a cognate advantage there reflects real learning of new forms.

title: Cross-language competition and the Revised Hierarchical Model

blocks.main: **Eye movements in a visual world task can reveal whether similar L1 words are active while bilinguals process L2.** In McMurray and colleagues’ study, competition between BEAR and PEAR depended on distance from the category boundary. **Allopenna and colleagues (1994)** found the **cohort effect**. Words that share a beginning with the target, such as beetle for beaker, draw early looks.
blocks.end: So looks to an object measure how active its name is, even when the final choice is correct.

blocks.main: **Marian and Spivey (2003) found that Russian words are active when Russian-English bilinguals listen in English, but not the reverse.** If L1 words are always activated, bilinguals hearing “speaker” in English should look at matches. The Russian word for matches, spichki, starts the same way. With one competitor present, they looked at within-language and between-language competitors to the same extent.
sub: With both competitors present, they looked at the within-language competitor more. They still looked at the between-language competitor about twice as often as a control object.
In Russian, English words did not seem to be activated. The small difference from the control was not statistically significant.
blocks.end: So competition between the languages is **asymmetric**, running from L1 into L2.

blocks.main: **Kroll and Stewart’s Revised Hierarchical Model explains the asymmetry with spreading activation.** The model has an L1 lexicon, an L2 lexicon and shared concepts. The L1 lexicon is larger and more strongly connected to concepts. The L2 lexicon has strong forward connections to the L1 lexicon, because that direction is emphasized in learning.
sub: Here Russian is the L1 and English is the L2.
In the English task, the concept for “speaker” partly activates the Russian word for matches, spichki.
Spichki is strongly linked to the concept for matches, so that activity feeds back to the concept. Conceptual activation for matches then leads to eye movements toward the matches.
blocks.end: In the L1 task, the conceptual links from L2 words are too weak to create this interference reliably.

blocks.main: **The model predicts that even balanced bilinguals are not two monolinguals in one.** For **balanced bilinguals**, conceptual links are similarly strong for both languages. So competitive dynamics and inhibition are engaged all the time.
blocks.end: So this prediction led to much work on bilinguals’ advantages in non-linguistic **cognitive control** tasks.

questions.q: What was Marian and Spivey’s hypothesis, and how did they test it?
questions.a: They hypothesized that if L1 words are always activated, Russian speakers should look at matches when hearing “speaker” in English. The Russian word for matches, spichki, begins like speaker. They tracked eye movements to such between-language competitors in a visual world display.

questions.q: What did Marian and Spivey find during L2 spoken word recognition?
questions.a: With one competitor present, bilinguals looked at within-language and between-language competitors to the same extent. With both present, they looked at the within-language competitor more. They still looked at the between-language competitor about twice as often as a control, so L1 words were active during L2 listening.

questions.q: What did Marian and Spivey find during L1 spoken word recognition?
questions.a: English words did not seem to be activated when native Russian speakers did the task in Russian. The small difference between the between-language and control conditions was not statistically significant. So the interference is asymmetric.

questions.q: What does the Revised Hierarchical Model assume about the two lexicons and their links?
questions.a: It assumes the L1 lexicon is larger and more strongly connected to relevant concepts. The L2 lexicon has strong forward connections to the L1 lexicon. So activation spreads more readily from an L2 word to an L1 word than the other way, because learners practice that direction.

questions.q: How does the Revised Hierarchical Model explain the Marian and Spivey results?
questions.a: In the L2 task, Russian and English bilinguals hear “speaker” in English. The concept for speaker partly activates the Russian word for matches, spichki. Russian is the L1, so spichki has a strong conceptual link, and it activates the concept of matches. That conceptual activation draws the eyes to the matches. In the L1 task, English words have weak conceptual links, so they cannot create this interference reliably.

questions.q: What counter-intuitive prediction does the model make for balanced bilinguals?
questions.a: It predicts that balanced bilinguals are not two monolinguals in one. Their conceptual links are similarly strong for both languages, so both languages compete and inhibition is engaged all the time. This led to much work on bilinguals’ advantages in non-linguistic cognitive control tasks.

title: Can a second language replace the first?

blocks.main: **Korean adoptees raised in French homes showed no trace of Korean on any test.** Korean has a **three-way stop contrast**, where stops at one place come in three kinds, **plain**, **tense** and **aspirated**. So pul (fire), Pul (horn) and phul (grass) are different words that differ only in the first stop. **Ventureyra and colleagues** found that adoptees were no better than monolingual French speakers at hearing these contrasts, while Korean speakers heard them nearly every time.
sub: Pallier and colleagues also found adoptees no better at recognizing Korean, choosing Korean translations, or detecting repeated excerpts.
Listening to French activated the classical language network in both groups. Subtracting Korean from French revealed no difference between the groups.
blocks.end: So when L1 is removed from the environment entirely, L2 can appear to replace it completely.

blocks.main: **Competitive dynamics offer one account of replacement.** L1 can be treated as a set of connections within and between brain regions. If those connections are never activated again, L2 could take them over, much as one eye takes over the other eye’s cortex in amblyopia.
blocks.end: So the open question is whether traces of L1 are left that can be salvaged by later learning.

blocks.main: **Terry Au’s group found that childhood overhearers of Spanish kept an advantage in pronunciation but not in grammar.** The students had overheard Spanish often as children but never spoke it. They began Spanish classes at about 14 and were tested after second-year college Spanish. Their VOT and accents were more native-like than those of typical late learners.
sub: The two groups differ in many ways. Korean is rarely heard in France, but Spanish is common in Los Angeles. Spanish may be a heritage language, and Spanish and English share cognates and a writing system.
blocks.end: So replacement may not be complete, since residual knowledge can be unmasked by later learning. Languages and learning situations differ in ways that are hard to control in experiments.

questions.q: What did Pallier and colleagues find about Korean adoptees raised in France?
questions.a: They found no remaining trace of Korean. Adoptees were no better than French speakers at recognizing Korean, picking Korean translations or detecting repeated excerpts. Brain imaging also treated Korean like any foreign language, so L2 appeared to replace L1 completely.

questions.q: What did Ventureyra and colleagues find with the Korean stop contrast?
questions.a: They found that Korean adoptees in France were no better than monolingual French speakers at the Korean stop contrasts. Korean speakers heard these differences nearly every time. Both adoptees and French speakers did well on a vowel contrast, so the problem was specific to the Korean stops.

questions.q: What did Terry Au’s group find with childhood overhearers of Spanish?
questions.a: They found that overhearers had more native-like pronunciation than typical late learners after two years of college Spanish. Their VOT nearly matched native speakers. They had little or no advantage in grammar, so early overhearing left traces mainly in the sound system.

questions.q: Why are the adoptee and overhearer results hard to compare directly?
questions.a: They are hard to compare because the groups differ in many ways besides early exposure. Korean is rarely heard in France, but Spanish is common in Los Angeles and may be a heritage language. Spanish and English also share cognates and a writing system, which Korean and French do not.

title: Sensitive periods for L2, Johnson and Newport and the critiques

blocks.main: **Second language learning is a model system for sensitive period research.** **Lenneberg (1967)** tied the sensitive period to the development of **cerebral dominance**, or language **laterality**. He drew on a rough alignment of brain development with language milestones and on resilience after brain injury or surgery.
sub: Much L1 evidence comes from idiosyncratic or rare cases.
Many people learn second languages at different ages with limited success. So those limits can be used to reason about the timing of the sensitive period.
blocks.end: So L2 learners give large, ordinary samples where L1 research has only rare cases.

blocks.main: **Johnson and Newport (1989) found that grammar scores fall with age of arrival up to puberty and become low and scattered after it.** They tested 46 native Korean or Chinese speakers who arrived in the United States between ages 3 and 39. An untimed **grammaticality judgment test** (GJT) asked whether recorded sentences were grammatical.
sub: Items tested rules such as plurals, the progressive -ing, determiners and question word order.
Early learners, up to about age 8, were often near-perfect and native-like.
Late arrivals showed a nearly random distribution of accuracy, unrelated to age of arrival.
blocks.end: The age effect was not explained by amount of experience, motivation, self-consciousness or American identification.

blocks.main: **Johnson and Newport read their data as a critical period that extends to second languages, best fit by the maturational state hypothesis.** The dependence of attainment on age fits a loss of learning ability over development. After the period closes, attainment depends on idiosyncratic learning abilities, so late learners vary widely.
sub: The **exercise hypothesis** says the early capacity declines only if it is not exercised. If it is exercised, language learning ability stays intact for life.
The **maturational state hypothesis** says the capacity declines with maturation whether or not it was exercised.
All the learners had exercised their capacity on an L1, yet later arrivals did worse. So the data fit the maturational state hypothesis.
blocks.end: This changes how the L1 data are read, because in cases like Genie both hypotheses predict poor learning.

blocks.main: **Ellis (2005) argued that an untimed GJT may measure explicit knowledge rather than grammar acquisition.** **Implicit knowledge** is intuitive and procedural. It is used automatically in fluent performance, cannot be put into words, and may be learnable only within the critical period. **Explicit knowledge** is conscious and declarative. It is used with controlled effort, can be put into words, and can be learned at any age.
sub: Untimed GJT performance was correlated with years of formal L2 education.
Starting age was related to the timed GJT, which limits the use of explicit rules.
blocks.end: So an age effect on an untimed GJT may partly reflect taught **metalinguistic** knowledge (conscious knowledge about language).

blocks.main: **Transfer and the language pairing change the age pattern.** Not all grammar is equally hard. The progressive -ing and word order are easiest, which matches children’s order of learning. Determiners are hard, and Chinese has no determiners. Questions come late for children but are among the easiest structures for late learners.
sub: **Birdsong and Molis (2001)** tested Spanish speakers learning English. Early arrivals scored near the top regardless of age, while late arrivals declined steadily with age.
That pattern is almost the reverse of the Chinese and Korean learners.
blocks.end: So age of arrival effects on the GJT may not reflect maturational constraints alone, because the first language matters.

blocks.main: **Overall, L2 attainment is lower for older learners, but how much lower depends on many factors.** It depends on which constructions are tested, how they are tested and the language pairing. It is hard to separate age from the amount and quality of experience. It is also hard to separate transfer from L2 acquisition, and performance from competence.
blocks.end: So these findings may not even deserve to be called conclusions.

questions.q: Why is L2 learning a useful model system for sensitive period research?
questions.a: It is useful because much L1 evidence comes from idiosyncratic or rare cases such as Genie or hemispherectomy. Many people learn second languages at different ages, often with limited success. So researchers can study large groups and use the limits of L2 success to reason about timing.

questions.q: What did Johnson and Newport (1989) do, and what patterns did they find?
questions.a: They gave an untimed grammaticality judgment test to 46 Korean or Chinese speakers who arrived in the United States between ages 3 and 39. Scores fell steadily with age of arrival up to puberty, and the earliest learners were native-like. After puberty, scores were low and nearly random with respect to age of arrival.

questions.q: Which version of the critical period hypothesis do Johnson and Newport’s data support, and why?
questions.a: Their data support the maturational state hypothesis. All of their learners had exercised their language capacity on an L1, yet later arrivals still learned English less well. The exercise hypothesis would predict that an exercised capacity stays intact, so it does not fit.

questions.q: What is the difference between implicit and explicit knowledge, according to Ellis (2005)?
questions.a: Implicit knowledge is intuitive and procedural, used automatically in fluent speech, and cannot be put into words. Explicit knowledge is conscious and declarative, used with controlled effort, and can be put into words. Implicit knowledge may only be learnable within the critical period, while explicit knowledge can be learned at any age.

questions.q: Why might an untimed GJT not measure grammar acquisition?
questions.a: An untimed GJT lets people take their time and apply conscious rules, so it allows explicit metalinguistic knowledge. Untimed GJT scores were correlated with years of formal L2 education. So an age effect on it may partly reflect taught knowledge rather than acquired grammar.

questions.q: What did Birdsong and Molis (2001) find, and what does it mean for maturational accounts?
questions.a: They found that Spanish speakers who arrived early scored near the top regardless of age, while late arrivals declined steadily with age. This is almost the reverse of Johnson and Newport’s Chinese and Korean learners. So the age pattern depends on the language pairing, which weakens a purely maturational account.
